sourceNotes: Seeded from FTDM roleplay performance indicators and finance cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: FTDM event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the finance cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Present value of a project's future cash flows divided by its initial outlay, so 1.15 means $1.15 of present value bought per $1 spent; anything below 1.0 is rejected and the ratio ranks projects when the budget is capped.
terms.whyItMatters: When an FTDM case hands the team a fixed capital budget and four projects, ranking by NPV overspends the budget — the index is what picks the combination that fits it.

terms.definition: Time until a project's cumulative *discounted* cash flows recover the outlay, so a project that pays back in 3.0 plain years may take 3.8 once each year's inflow is divided by (1+r)^n.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges push back on a team that quotes plain payback for a five-year equipment case; the discounted figure is the one that survives a follow-up about the time value of money.

terms.definition: The discount rate at which two mutually exclusive projects have identical net present values; below it the longer-lived project wins and above it the front-loaded one does, which is why NPV and IRR can disagree.
terms.whyItMatters: A case that gives two projects and a cost of capital is really asking which side of this rate the firm sits on — that single comparison decides the recommendation.

terms.definition: Rate that grows the outlay into the future value of the inflows when those inflows are reinvested at the cost of capital rather than at the project's own IRR, so it lands below a flattering IRR and removes the multiple-root problem.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case project shows a 34% IRR against a 9% cost of capital, the recomputed figure is the defensible number to present — the raw IRR silently assumes 34% reinvestment.

terms.definition: A project's NPV spread into a level yearly amount by dividing it by the annuity factor for its life, which is the only fair way to compare a 4-year machine against a 7-year one.
terms.whyItMatters: Replacement-equipment cases deliberately give unequal lives; comparing raw NPVs there is the trap, and the annualized figure is the answer judges are listening for.

terms.definition: The lump sum standing in for every cash flow past the explicit forecast, usually final-year flow times (1+g) divided by (WACC minus g); it routinely carries 60-80% of a DCF's total value, so the g assumption dominates the answer.
terms.whyItMatters: In a valuation case, moving growth from 2% to 3% against a 9% discount rate swings this figure by roughly a sixth — the team that names that sensitivity wins the question.

terms.definition: Blended required return computed as the equity weight times the cost of equity plus the debt weight times the after-tax cost of debt, using market-value weights rather than book values.
terms.whyItMatters: Every discounting decision in an FTDM capital-budgeting case runs through this one number, and using book weights or a pre-tax debt rate quietly changes the accept/reject verdict.

terms.definition: The coupon or yield multiplied by (1 minus the tax rate), because interest is deductible — an 8% note at a 25% rate costs the firm 6%, and that gap is the whole tax shield.
terms.whyItMatters: A team that plugs the stated 8% into a WACC calculation overstates the discount rate and rejects a project the case intends them to accept.

terms.definition: Underwriting and issuance fees that shrink the net proceeds of a new security sale, so a $30 share netting $27.60 raises the cost of *new* equity above the cost of retained earnings by roughly the same 8%.
terms.whyItMatters: Financing-mix cases ask why a firm exhausts retained earnings before issuing stock; this cost is the arithmetic reason, not a preference.

terms.term: Marginal cost of capital break point
terms.definition: The dollar level of new financing at which the blended cost steps up, found by dividing the retained earnings available by the equity weight — $6M of retained earnings at a 60% equity weight breaks at $10M raised.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case lists a capital budget larger than internal funds, this is the calculation that shows which projects are still above the hurdle once the cheaper money runs out.

terms.definition: Systematic risk stripped of capital structure — levered beta divided by [1 + (1 - tax rate)(debt/equity)] — so a peer's risk can be relevered at the subject firm's own debt load.
terms.whyItMatters: Valuing a private target from public comparables requires this two-step unlever/relever, and skipping it imports the comparable's leverage into the target's cost of equity.

terms.definition: Total contribution margin divided by operating income, giving the multiple by which EBIT moves for a 1% sales move — a factor of 3.0 turns a 10% sales drop into a 30% EBIT collapse.
terms.whyItMatters: Fixed-versus-variable cost cases hinge on this multiple: it is the number that tells the team whether automating the plant is survivable in a downturn.

terms.definition: EBIT divided by (EBIT minus interest), measuring how far each 1% change in operating income is amplified into earnings per share — $500K EBIT against $200K interest gives 1.67x.
terms.whyItMatters: Recapitalization cases ask whether more debt helps shareholders; this ratio quantifies the added EPS volatility that comes with the higher expected EPS.

terms.definition: Total borrowings less cash, divided by trailing operating cash earnings, expressed as a multiple of years to repay; lenders and rating agencies commonly draw the investment-grade line near 3.0x and distress near 5.0x.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case asks whether a firm can fund an acquisition with debt, computing the pro forma multiple against that 3.0x line is the decision, not a talking point.

terms.definition: Equity market capitalization plus total debt and preferred stock, minus cash and equivalents — the price of the whole operating business regardless of who financed it, which is why it pairs with EBIT or EBITDA and never with net income.
terms.whyItMatters: Mismatching this with a bottom-line earnings figure is the classic multiple error judges probe; the cash subtraction alone can move a target's implied price several percent.

terms.definition: The excess above an unaffected trading price paid to acquire a majority stake, historically 20-40%, justified by the buyer's new power to change management, capital structure and dividend policy.
terms.whyItMatters: A comparable-company valuation gives a minority-basis price; an acquisition case must add this percentage before the offer is credible to the judge playing the seller.

terms.definition: A reduction of roughly 20-35% applied to a private company's indicated value because the shares cannot be sold quickly at a quoted price, applied after any minority or control adjustment.
terms.whyItMatters: Family-business succession and buy-sell cases turn on this haircut; quoting a public multiple with no such adjustment overvalues the stake by a quarter.

terms.definition: A P/E divided by the expected annual earnings growth rate in percentage points, so a 30 P/E growing 30% scores 1.0; under 1.0 is conventionally read as cheap relative to growth and over 2.0 as rich.
terms.whyItMatters: It settles the case argument that a high-multiple stock is automatically overpriced — the team that computes it can defend paying 30 times earnings.

terms.definition: Return above the risk-free rate divided by the portfolio's standard deviation, converting raw performance into reward per unit of total risk — 12% return, 3% risk-free and 15% volatility gives 0.60.
terms.whyItMatters: Client-portfolio roleplays give two funds with different returns and volatilities; this single number is how the team justifies recommending the lower-returning one.

terms.definition: The straight line plotting required return against beta, anchored at the risk-free rate and passing through the market portfolio; a security plotting above it is underpriced and one below it is overpriced.
terms.whyItMatters: It converts a beta and an expected return into a buy-or-sell recommendation, which is exactly what an investment-advisory roleplay asks the team to deliver.

terms.definition: A decomposition of return on equity into net profit margin times asset turnover times the equity multiplier, so two firms with an identical 15% ROE can be shown to earn it from margin, efficiency or debt.
terms.whyItMatters: When a case gives ROE that improved year over year, this breakdown reveals whether the gain came from operations or from levering up — the distinction the judge is testing.

terms.definition: Net income minus operating cash flow, divided by average total assets; a large positive value means reported profit is not arriving as cash and predicts weaker future earnings.
terms.whyItMatters: Given an income statement and a cash flow statement in a case, this is the one calculation that turns a vague suspicion about earnings quality into evidence.

terms.definition: Pro forma test of whether a merger raises or lowers the acquirer's earnings per share; in an all-stock deal it is accretive whenever the acquirer's P/E exceeds the target's, before synergies.
terms.whyItMatters: Acquisition roleplays hand the team both P/Es and a share count — computing the combined EPS is what separates a recommendation from an opinion.

terms.definition: A self-imposed ceiling on total investment spending that forces a firm to reject positive-NPV projects, making the task selecting the highest-value bundle that fits rather than approving everything above the hurdle.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the constraint that makes an FTDM project-selection case a real decision; without it the team would simply accept every project with a positive NPV.

terms.definition: The minimum acceptable return a proposal must clear, set at the cost of capital plus any risk adjustment for the specific project, and compared against IRR rather than against accounting return.
terms.whyItMatters: Cases often set this above WACC for a risky new line; noticing the adjustment is what stops a team from approving a project that only clears the corporate average.

terms.definition: Valuing a business by applying trading multiples of similar public firms — matched on industry, size, growth and margin — to the subject's own metric, producing a range rather than a point estimate.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the fastest defensible valuation in a timed roleplay, and the judge's follow-up is always how the peer set was chosen.

terms.definition: How much of reported profit is backed by recurring cash from operations rather than by one-time gains, accounting estimates or accrual timing — high quality means net income and operating cash flow track each other.
terms.whyItMatters: Due-diligence cases ask why a profitable target is a bad buy; this is the framing that lets a team point at the cash flow statement instead of the income statement.

terms.definition: A financial statement reporting the cash flowing into and out of a business over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash flow reveals whether a business can pay its bills even when it reports a profit.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: A dependency network that estimates each task's expected duration as optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic, divided by six — a weighted three-point estimate for work with uncertain durations, unlike a critical path calculation, which assumes one fixed duration per task.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you three time estimates for a task and ask for the expected duration; the weighted formula, not a plain average of the three numbers, is the scored answer.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Direct labor plus manufacturing overhead — the spending required to turn raw materials into finished goods. It deliberately excludes direct materials, which is what separates it from prime cost, defined as direct materials plus direct labor; the two overlap on labor and therefore cannot be added together to reach total product cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost questions ask candidates to sort a list of factory charges into the two groupings, and the shared labor term is where most answers collapse.

terms.definition: The process section 553 of the Administrative Procedure Act requires before an agency may issue a binding legislative rule: publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register, take public comment for a stated period, respond to the significant comments, and publish the final rule with a statement of basis and purpose, normally effective 30 days later. A rule adopted without those steps can be vacated as procedurally invalid even when its substance is sound.
terms.whyItMatters: Administrative-law questions ask how an industry trade group can influence a regulation before it ever binds its members.

terms.definition: A shortcut that estimates how many years an investment takes to double by dividing 72 by the annual percentage return.
terms.whyItMatters: Investing roleplays reward a competitor who can tell a client on the spot that 8% doubles their money in about nine years.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: A horizontal bar timeline showing each task's start, duration and overlap against calendar dates; it displays schedule but not logic, whereas a PERT network draws the dependency arrows that reveal which tasks actually control the finish date.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-management roleplays ask which tool to bring to a status meeting: the bar timeline communicates progress to a client, but it cannot answer which delay pushes the deadline.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: The fixed sequence a period's records travel — analyze source documents, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance, adjust, prepare statements, then close temporary accounts into equity. The order is not optional: statements are drawn before closing, and closing is what resets revenue and expense accounts to zero for the next period.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items present the steps scrambled and ask what comes immediately after the adjusting entries are posted.

terms.definition: Witte's account of why a fear appeal sometimes backfires. The audience first appraises the threat - how severe it is and how likely it is to hit them - and then appraises efficacy: whether the recommended action actually works and whether they can personally perform it. High threat with high efficacy produces danger control and the behaviour changes; high threat with low efficacy produces fear control, where people reduce the fear instead of the risk by denying, avoiding or mocking the message. Raising the threat without raising efficacy makes the outcome worse than saying nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A workplace-safety or public-service roleplay is scored on pairing the alarming statistic with one specific step the audience can carry out, and this names why the pairing is required.

terms.definition: The rate applied to the next dollar earned, which is the top bracket a taxpayer reaches rather than the rate paid on all of their income.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-liability items test whether a raise into a higher bracket taxes the whole salary at the new rate — it does not, only the dollars above the bracket line.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: Summing durations along every dependency chain and taking the longest one as the shortest possible project duration; every task on it has zero float, so any slip there slips the whole project, while a delay off it is absorbed.
terms.whyItMatters: A project roleplay that asks which of several late tasks to escalate is answered by locating the zero-float chain, because effort spent on the others buys no finish-date improvement.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: Estimated total overhead for the coming year divided by the estimated total of an allocation base such as machine hours or direct labor hours, computed before the period begins so jobs can be costed the day they finish. Because both inputs are estimates, actual spending leaves overhead over- or underapplied at year end, and that difference must be closed out.
terms.whyItMatters: Job-costing items ask for the full cost of an order completed in March, long before the year's real overhead is known.

terms.definition: Overestimating both the intensity and the duration of a future emotional reaction; the duration half alone is the durability bias, and the two named causes are focalism -- attending only to the focal event and not to everything else that will fill the day -- and immune neglect, discounting how quickly one rationalizes an outcome. Lottery winners and people newly paralyzed converge far closer than either group predicts.
terms.whyItMatters: A risk-of-personal-decisions item asking whether a competitor should take a demanding promotion is testing this: the answer that survives is one that weighs the ordinary days after the change, not the peak of the reaction to it.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing a business's assets, liabilities, and equity at a single point in time.
terms.whyItMatters: The balance sheet is where competitors read financial position and solvency.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: A deliverable-oriented decomposition of a project into progressively smaller work packages governed by the 100 percent rule — the children of any element must sum to exactly that element, no more and no less — so it captures scope, not sequence, which the schedule adds afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how to start planning a project, the accepted first move is decomposing deliverables before estimating or scheduling, and the completeness rule is what stops forgotten work becoming a budget overrun.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Overhead assignment that first pools costs by activity — machine setups, inspections, purchase orders — then charges each product using that activity's own cost driver. It corrects the distortion of a single plantwide rate spread on direct labor hours, which systematically overcosts high-volume simple products and undercosts low-volume complex ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost roleplays about a specialty item that looks profitable under the old allocation and loses money under the new one are testing exactly that reversal.

terms.definition: The stepped route a complaint travels under a collective bargaining agreement — usually the immediate supervisor, then department management with a union steward, then a company-wide review, ending in binding arbitration by a neutral third party whose decision both sides accepted in advance. Each step carries its own filing deadline, and missing one can forfeit the claim regardless of merit.
terms.whyItMatters: A union-workplace roleplay is scored on routing the complaint through the contract's steps rather than settling it informally with the employee.

terms.definition: Total tax paid divided by total income, always lower than the top bracket a taxpayer falls in because earlier dollars were taxed at lower rates.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives income and tax owed and asks for the rate actually paid; answering with the bracket rate is the trap.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: Latest allowable start minus earliest possible start for a task — the delay it can absorb before the project finish moves; total float is shared along a chain, whereas free float is the smaller amount that delays no immediately following task at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a network with early and late start dates, exam questions ask how long a task can slip; confusing the shared allowance with the task-level one over-promises the client in a status roleplay.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: Software running sales, purchasing, inventory, payroll, and accounting off one shared database, so a single shipment posts to inventory, receivables, and the general ledger in one transaction. The gain over separate applications is that nobody re-keys data between them, which removes an entire class of reconciliation errors.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology questions ask why a growing firm outgrows standalone bookkeeping software once its departments each keep their own records.

terms.definition: The computational discovery of patterns and correlations hidden in large datasets.
terms.whyItMatters: Mining surfaces competitive insights that simple reports would miss.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing revenue, expenses, and profit over a period of time.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the primary tool for judging whether operations are profitable.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: Comparing budgeted cost of work actually completed against what was spent and what was planned: cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost, schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value, and any index below 1.0 signals over budget or behind schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-evaluation items ask whether a project that has spent sixty percent of its budget is in trouble; only the ratio against work completed answers it, and a raw spending percentage does not.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: A predetermined benchmark for what one unit of input should cost and how much of it should be used, against which actual results are measured. The total gap decomposes into a price variance — actual price minus standard price, times actual quantity — and a quantity variance — actual quantity minus standard quantity, times standard price — so a purchasing decision and a production problem are never blamed on the same manager.
terms.whyItMatters: Manufacturing budget questions supply both actual and standard figures and expect the gap split across the two responsible departments.

terms.definition: Optimizes the discounted value of a customer's entire future stream of purchases and will accept a thinner margin on any single sale to protect it, whereas transactional marketing maximizes margin on each separate exchange and budgets acquisition and retention as unrelated lines; the two approaches give opposite answers to whether a long-standing customer should be granted a concession on one order.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a loyal customer asks for an exception is decided by which of the two frames you argue from, and judges expect the alternative named.

terms.definition: An amount subtracted directly from tax owed, so it is worth its full face value — unlike a deduction, which only reduces the income the tax is figured on.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a $1,000 credit with a $1,000 deduction and ask which saves more; the credit does, by the taxpayer's bracket rate.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Inspecting a randomly drawn sample from a delivered lot and accepting or rejecting the entire lot on the count of defects found, against a stated acceptable quality level — the highest defect percentage treated as satisfactory — which trades a known risk of passing a bad lot for the cost of inspecting every unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Receiving-process questions ask how a buyer verifies a large shipment economically; naming the tolerable defect percentage and the risk it accepts is what distinguishes a full answer from 'check some of them'.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: The determination of whether a person is an employee or an independent contractor, made under the IRS common-law control test weighing behavioral control, financial control, and the nature of the relationship. An employee receives a Form W-2 with taxes withheld and the employer's matching payroll tax paid; a contractor receives a Form 1099-NEC and carries the full self-employment tax alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Payroll roleplays about a long-serving contractor who works set hours on company equipment test the control factors and the back-tax exposure of getting them wrong.

terms.definition: An orderly, methodical approach to tasks and decisions that follows a logical structure.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges favor structured reasoning over a scattered approach.

terms.definition: Profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price, taxable only once the sale happens and taxed at a lower rate when the asset was held over a year.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios ask whether a client owes tax on a stock that has risen in value; unrealized gains are not taxed until sold.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: Charting sample measurements over time against limits computed from the process's own variation to separate common-cause noise from assignable-cause shifts; it monitors a process while it runs, unlike acceptance sampling, which judges a finished lot after the fact.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method roleplays ask how to catch a drifting machine before it produces scrap; watching the charted trend is the in-process answer, and inspecting finished goods is the one judges mark as too late.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: A projected or adjusted statement built on stated assumptions — next year's forecast, or reported results excluding items management labels non-recurring. It is neither audited nor GAAP, and SEC Regulation G requires a public company publishing any such figure to reconcile it to the nearest GAAP measure so readers can see precisely what was removed.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a startup's projections for a lender, and exam items about a press release touting adjusted earnings, both turn on the unaudited status of this statement.

terms.definition: Elkington's reporting frame measuring a firm on three accounts — profit, people, and planet — so that social and environmental results are stated in their own units alongside net income rather than folded into it as goodwill or a marketing expense.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask what a sustainability report adds beyond the income statement, and the answer is the two non-financial accounts named explicitly.

terms.definition: How easily an asset can be converted to cash without losing much value.
terms.whyItMatters: Liquidity explains why a profitable business can still run short of cash.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: Unloading inbound freight and transferring it directly to outbound trailers within hours, sorting by destination on the dock, so the goods are never put away — the opposite of conventional warehousing, which stores, picks and holds stock and therefore incurs carrying cost that this eliminates.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about cutting inventory cost and speeding delivery expect this as the named technique, and the judge wants the requirement that inbound and outbound schedules be tightly synchronized.

terms.definition: Extra output produced by one more worker, computed as the change in quantity divided by the change in workers. Going from 4 to 5 employees and from 40 to 46 units gives 6. It also sets marginal cost: at a $120 daily wage, that worker's units cost 120 ÷ 6 = $20 each, so cost per unit rises the moment the added output starts shrinking.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing and productivity items ask what one more scheduled worker actually adds and what that output costs, which is where diminishing returns become dollars.

terms.definition: A document a seller issues to request payment for goods or services provided.
terms.whyItMatters: Invoices drive accounts-receivable timing and payment terms.

terms.definition: A legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law roleplays turn on whether promises, rights, and duties are enforceable.

terms.definition: Matching a checkbook or ledger against a bank statement by adjusting both sides — outstanding checks and deposits in transit on the bank's, fees and interest on the depositor's.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives a statement balance and a book balance and asks for the true cash figure; only adjusting one side gets it wrong.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: Boundaries drawn three standard deviations above and below the process mean and calculated FROM the process's own output, which makes them a statement of what the process does — specification limits are set by the customer or engineer and state what the product must be, so a process can sit inside one pair and outside the other.
terms.whyItMatters: The classic exam trap shows points inside the charted band but outside customer tolerance; recognizing that a stable process can still be producing unacceptable parts is the tested discrimination.

terms.definition: Keep producing while the revenue the next unit brings in exceeds the cost it adds, and stop at the output where the two are equal. If the next unit adds $12 of revenue and $9 of cost, making it gains $3; past the crossing point each extra unit subtracts from profit even though total revenue is still rising.
terms.whyItMatters: Factors-affecting-profit items ask for the quantity a firm should produce from a marginal cost and marginal revenue schedule, not from total revenue.

terms.definition: Current assets minus current liabilities — a measure of short-term financial health.
terms.whyItMatters: Working capital shows whether a business can cover immediate obligations.

terms.definition: A classical four-question procedure for locating the exact point at which two sides disagree: conjecture (did it happen?), definition (what should it be called?), quality (how serious is it?) and policy (what should be done about it?). Arguing at the wrong level is the standard failure - answering 'what should we do' while the other side is still disputing whether anything happened produces two speeches that never touch.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge in a conflict roleplay disputes your facts and you answer with a solution, you lose points for never meeting the objection; this names the level you skipped.

terms.definition: Paying a loan off through fixed installments split between interest and principal, with the interest share largest at the start and shrinking every payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why an early mortgage payment barely reduces the balance; the amortization split is the reason, not a fee.

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: Amplification of demand variability moving upstream, where a small retail sales swing becomes a larger distributor order swing and a still larger factory order swing, driven by batch ordering, price promotions, forecast updating and shortage gaming — shared point-of-sale data damps it.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays use this to justify sharing real sales data with suppliers, and the four named causes are what turn a vague answer about 'communication' into a scored one.

terms.definition: Keep the doors open in the short run only while price covers average variable cost; at a lower price closing loses less, because fixed costs are owed either way. At $8 price with $7 variable and $4 fixed cost per unit, the firm loses $3 a unit but still operates, since shutting down would lose the full $4.
terms.whyItMatters: Operating-cost roleplays ask whether a location losing money should close now; the test is variable cost coverage, not whether the site is profitable.

terms.definition: Recording revenue or expense when it is incurred, not when cash changes hands.
terms.whyItMatters: Accrual accounting reveals true profitability beyond the cash view.

terms.definition: The ability to understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
terms.whyItMatters: It underlies teamwork, service, and conflict-resolution answers.

terms.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities, the standard test of whether a business can cover what it owes within the next twelve months.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand over a balance sheet and ask whether the firm can meet short-term obligations; a ratio under 1.0 is the answer that says no.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: The width of the customer's tolerance divided by six standard deviations of process spread, with Cpk penalizing an off-center mean by measuring only the nearer specification limit; 1.33 is the common minimum and a value below 1.0 means defects are unavoidable even when the process is perfectly stable.
terms.whyItMatters: Supplier-quality roleplays use this figure as the acceptance bar: a supplier can hold a steady process and still fail, which is the argument you make when resolving a quality dispute.

terms.definition: Selling price multiplied by the extra output the next worker adds — $15 a unit times 6 units is $90 a day. Hire while that figure is at or above the wage and stop when it drops below: at a $100 wage this worker is not worth adding, even though the worker before, adding 9 units and $135, clearly was.
terms.whyItMatters: Labor and productivity questions ask how many people a firm should employ, and the comparison of this figure to the wage is the tested rule.

terms.definition: Money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services already received.
terms.whyItMatters: Payables shape the cash position competitors must manage.

terms.definition: The secret-ballot vote that decides union representation: a petition requires authorization cards from at least 30% of the proposed bargaining unit, and certification follows a simple majority of ballots actually cast, not of the unit — 40 votes for out of 70 cast in a 100-person unit certifies the union. A valid election bars another for 12 months, and a resulting contract bars one for up to three years.
terms.whyItMatters: Organizing roleplays test the 30% showing of interest against the majority needed to win, a pair of numbers competitors frequently collapse into one.

terms.definition: Current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities — the stricter liquidity test, because inventory may not convert to cash in time to pay a bill.
terms.whyItMatters: A retailer with a healthy current ratio and a weak quick ratio is the classic exam case, and the difference is inventory the business cannot sell fast.

terms.definition: Time spent handling contacts and wrap-up divided by time logged in and available — 45 minutes of work inside a 50-minute available hour is 90%. Utilization puts total paid hours in the denominator instead, so it absorbs breaks, training and meetings and always reads lower; sustained occupancy above roughly 85% is the figure that predicts agent burnout.
terms.whyItMatters: A staffing roleplay judged on turnover risk needs the two denominators kept apart, or the schedule looks comfortable on paper and burns the team out.

terms.definition: Unit price plus freight, insurance, duties and tariffs, customs brokerage, and handling to the receiving dock — the total that makes an offshore quote comparable to a domestic one, which is why the lower quoted unit price frequently loses once every downstream charge is added.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays present a cheaper overseas bid and expect you to reject a comparison based on quoted price alone by adding the delivery-related charges before deciding.

terms.definition: The smallest output at which long-run average cost stops falling and flattens out. If unit cost drops from $9 to $6 between 10,000 and 50,000 units and then holds at $6, the threshold is 50,000 — a rival producing 20,000 pays $7 or $8 and cannot match a $6.50 price, which is how the number becomes an entry barrier.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition items ask why a small entrant cannot match an incumbent's price, and the expected answer is the output threshold, not brand loyalty.

terms.definition: A list of all ledger accounts and balances used to check that debits equal credits.
terms.whyItMatters: Trial balances verify the accuracy of financial records in case work.

terms.definition: The final digit of a code such as a twelve-digit UPC, computed from the digits before it so a scanner can catch its own misread: multiply the digits in odd positions by three, add the digits in even positions, and choose the last digit that lifts the total to the next multiple of ten.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-records questions ask how a scanner knows a keyed-in barcode was mistyped without any lookup, and this arithmetic is the mechanism.

terms.definition: A tax structure whose rate rises as income rises, taxing each band of income at its own rate — the opposite of a regressive tax that takes a larger share from lower earners.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-structure questions ask competitors to classify income tax, sales tax and payroll tax, and sales tax is regressive despite its single rate.

terms.definition: The share of paid staff time not available to take contacts — breaks, training, meetings, absence and paid leave. A center budgeting 30% shrinkage must schedule about 1.43 bodies for every agent it needs live on the phones, because 1 divided by 0.70 is 1.43; ignoring it understaffs a peak by roughly a third.
terms.whyItMatters: Peaks-in-demand roleplays ask how many people to put on the schedule, and the gross-up is where the answer is won or lost.

terms.definition: An international quality-management standard certifying that documented processes exist, are followed and are audited by an independent registrar with surveillance visits — it certifies the management SYSTEM, not the product, so a registered firm can lawfully make a mediocre item consistently.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays treat registration as evidence of process discipline, and the judge is listening for the caveat that it guarantees consistency rather than excellence.

terms.definition: Gap between what buyers would have paid and what they did pay, measured as the area under the demand curve and above the market price. With demand starting at $50, a $20 price and 300 units sold, it equals ½ × 300 × ($50 − $20) = $4,500 — and a price rise to $30 cuts it, which is the value a seller captures when it segments buyers.
terms.whyItMatters: Price-function questions ask what buyers lose when a price rises or a shortage appears; the triangle turns that into a dollar figure.

terms.definition: The dollar gap between inventory valued under FIFO and the same inventory valued under LIFO — FIFO inventory minus LIFO inventory — disclosed in the notes so a reader can restate a LIFO firm's inventory and cost of goods sold onto a FIFO basis before comparing it with anyone else.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand you a footnote figure and ask you to compare two competitors' inventory when one uses LIFO and one uses FIFO; the comparison means nothing until the reserve is added back.

terms.definition: A brand's own market share divided by the share of its single largest competitor — 20% against a leader's 40% is 0.5x, and only the market leader can score above 1.0 — which is the horizontal axis of the growth-share matrix; two brands holding an identical absolute share therefore land in opposite quadrants depending on how dominant the rival directly above each of them happens to be.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that reports 20% share and calls it strong is answered by asking what the leader holds; the ratio, not the raw percentage, is what drives the portfolio decision.

terms.definition: Total liabilities divided by owner's equity, showing how much of the business is financed by lenders rather than owners and how exposed it is to a downturn.
terms.whyItMatters: Financing scenarios ask whether a firm can take on another loan, and a high ratio is the reason a lender says no.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: A control that releases payment only when the purchase order, the receiving report and the supplier invoice agree on item, quantity and price; any one document alone can be forged or wrong, so requiring all three is what blocks payment for goods never ordered or never delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounts-payable and ethics-in-purchasing roleplays ask what stops a fraudulent invoice from being paid, and naming all three documents plus the fields compared is the complete answer.

terms.definition: Area between the equal-shares diagonal and the actual income curve, divided by the whole triangle under that diagonal, giving 0 for identical incomes and 1 for one household holding everything. A move from 0.38 to 0.45 means income concentrated, and since it is a ratio it says nothing about whether anyone got richer.
terms.whyItMatters: Economic-development items compare two markets' income spread to pick a target segment, and the score is the measure they hand you.

terms.definition: Money owed to a business by customers for goods or services already delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: Receivables affect cash flow timing and collection decisions.

terms.definition: Standard measure of non-degree instruction in which one unit equals 10 contact hours of participation in an accredited program, so a two-day 16-hour seminar earns 1.6 units. A college credit hour is a different currency entirely — roughly 15 contact hours across a semester — and licensing boards rarely convert one into the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked on the exam to price a training plan against a 40-hour renewal requirement, a competitor has to convert seminar hours into units before the budget makes sense.

terms.definition: The payroll deduction funding Social Security and Medicare, taken at a fixed percentage of wages and matched dollar for dollar by the employer.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-stub interpretation items ask why gross pay minus income tax still does not equal take-home pay, and FICA is the missing line.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.term: Hazard analysis and critical control points
terms.definition: A seven-principle food-safety system that analyzes biological, chemical and physical hazards, fixes the specific steps where a hazard can be eliminated or controlled, sets a measurable critical limit at each such step, then monitors, corrects, verifies and records — control at those points, not final-product testing, is what proves safety.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about food handling reward naming the control step and its measurable limit — a cooking temperature or a holding time — instead of general cleanliness advice.

terms.definition: Allocate a budget so the last dollar spent on each good returns the same added satisfaction: MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py. If one item returns 20 utils per dollar and another 10, shifting spending toward the first raises total satisfaction until the two ratios meet — the rule that produces the downward-sloping demand curve.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior roleplays ask why a shopper walked away from the better product; the per-dollar comparison, not the raw benefit, explains the switch.

terms.definition: A write-down rule under ASC 330: inventory carried at historical cost must be reduced to replacement cost when that is lower, but never above net realizable value — selling price minus completion and disposal costs — nor below that ceiling minus a normal profit margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges ask what to do about obsolete stock still on the books at full cost; the answer is the mandatory write-down and the loss it forces onto this period's income statement.

terms.definition: The advisory power of specialists such as legal, HR, or IT to recommend and to be consulted, without the power to order action in another department; line authority is the direct command relationship over subordinates who produce the firm's goods or services.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe an HR manager whose hiring recommendation a plant manager overrode and ask which authority type each held.

terms.definition: Net income divided by owner's equity, measuring profit generated per dollar the owners have invested rather than per dollar of sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items compare two firms with equal profits and different equity bases; the one earning more per invested dollar wins.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: A company-wide philosophy making every employee responsible for continuous improvement and customer-defined quality; quality assurance is the narrower set of process activities designed to prevent defects, and quality control is the narrowest — the inspection and testing that finds defects after production.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items line up the three terms and ask which one an inspection station belongs to; sorting philosophy from prevention from detection is the whole question.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: An estimate of ending inventory made without a physical count: multiply net sales by the historical gross-profit percentage to approximate cost of goods sold, then subtract that from the cost of goods available for sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Insurance-claim and interim-statement questions give you sales figures and a prior-year margin but no count, and this is the only route to an inventory number a judge will accept.

terms.definition: Something of value exchanged between parties that makes a contract binding.
terms.whyItMatters: Without consideration, an agreement is a mere promise and not legally enforceable.

terms.definition: Net income available to common shareholders divided by shares outstanding, the per-share figure that lets companies of different sizes be compared.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios quote it as the headline number, and a competitor is expected to know a buyback raises it without any change in profit.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: An energy-control procedure requiring every power source to a machine to be isolated, physically locked, and tagged by the individual servicing it — with the rule that only that person may remove their own lock — so no one can restart equipment while a colleague is inside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment-safety roleplays about a maintenance injury expect this named procedure and the one-worker-one-lock rule, not general advice to turn the machine off.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: The difference between a budgeted amount and the actual amount spent or earned.
terms.whyItMatters: Variances flag where a plan and reality diverge, prompting corrective action.

terms.definition: A persuasive structure adapted from Carl Rogers' therapy: open by restating the opposing position accurately enough that its holder would accept your summary, name the conditions under which it is valid, and only then introduce your own claim and the ground the two share. It deliberately withholds the thesis until the audience has been disarmed, which makes it the standard choice for a hostile listener and a poor choice for one who already agrees and wants the recommendation in the first line.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which the judge plays an angry supervisor or a customer who has already refused once is scored on this opening move rather than on a louder restatement of your case.

terms.definition: A retirement account whose contributions escape tax now and whose withdrawals are taxed later, trading a deduction today for taxable income in retirement.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement-planning roleplays turn on when the client wants the tax bill, which is the whole traditional-versus-Roth decision.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: Outsourcing physical distribution functions — warehousing, transportation, freight handling — to a provider that owns trucks and buildings; a fourth-party provider owns no assets and instead manages the other providers, acting as a single coordinating layer over several third parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution-strategy questions ask which outsourcing level fits a firm that lacks not trucks but the ability to coordinate several carriers, and the asset-owning versus orchestrating split is the answer.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: Delivery terms placing title and risk of loss with the buyer the moment a carrier takes the goods, so the buyer adds the freight to inventory cost and reports goods still in transit at period end — the mirror of FOB destination, where the seller keeps both title and freight until delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: Cutoff questions ask which company reports a shipment sitting on a truck on December 31, and the answer turns entirely on which of the two terms the invoice names.

terms.term: Goleman's four-domain model of emotional intelligence
terms.definition: Sorts emotional competence into four domains — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — arranged as a 2x2 grid: the left column is personal competence (handling yourself), the right column is social competence (handling others), the top row is recognition and the bottom row is regulation. It is a mixed model of learnable workplace competencies, so it is assessed with a 360-degree rater inventory rather than with a right-answer test.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that lists four manager behaviors and asks which one is social awareness rather than relationship management is scored against this grid, and a management roleplay judge expects a candidate to name which domain a weakness sits in before proposing the fix.

terms.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share, the number of dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual profit — a rough gauge of how much growth is priced in.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a client on whether a stock looks expensive in an investing roleplay turns on this multiple, not on the share price alone.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: A structured visit by managers to the actual place work happens, to observe the process and ask questions rather than to inspect people or correct anyone on the spot — the no-blame, observe-only rule is what keeps workers from staging the process for the visitor.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a manager should diagnose a slow process, the expected answer is direct observation at the work site rather than a report or a meeting, which is what an operations judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: A bad-debt estimate built from a schedule that sorts every customer balance by days past due and applies a rising uncollectible rate to each bucket, targeting the ENDING allowance balance — unlike the percentage-of-sales approach, which computes the period's expense straight from revenue and ignores whatever already sits in the allowance.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam gives you an aging schedule plus an existing allowance balance, and the adjusting entry is the difference between them, not the computed total.

terms.definition: A rating form whose points are each defined by a real example of observable behavior — a 5 might read greets every guest within thirty seconds while a 2 reads acknowledges guests only after they approach — built from critical incidents gathered from people who do the job. A plain graphic rating scale labels the same points only excellent through poor, which is why two managers can rate identical behavior differently on it.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay complains that appraisals are inconsistent between supervisors, the tested fix is anchoring each scale point in described behavior.

terms.definition: A retirement account funded with money already taxed, whose qualified withdrawals — contributions and growth alike — come out tax-free.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a young client in a retirement roleplay usually points here, because decades of growth escape tax when the current bracket is low.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: A solicitation that describes a problem and invites vendors to propose their own solution, approach and price, evaluated on weighted criteria beyond cost — where a request for quotation specifies the exact item and quantity already and asks only for price and delivery, making it a lowest-bidder instrument.
terms.whyItMatters: Bid-process roleplays turn on choosing the right document: asking for solutions when you already know the specification wastes vendor effort, and asking only for price on an undefined need produces incomparable bids.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: A detail file holding one account per customer, vendor, or asset, whose balances must total exactly to the single control account carrying that category in the general ledger — the general ledger holds the summary figure that reaches the statements, this holds the per-name detail that supports it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking which specific customers owe the overdue balance is answered from this ledger; the trial balance shows only one combined receivable line.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: Annual dividends per share divided by share price, stating income return as a percentage so a dividend stock can be compared against a savings rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A client asking for income rather than growth in a retirement roleplay is asking about this figure, which moves whenever the share price moves.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Assigning each item a storage location based on picking velocity, unit weight and case cube, so the fastest-moving lines sit closest to packing at waist height — the objective is minimizing picker travel distance, which is the largest single component of order-fulfillment labor.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about slow order fulfillment expect a layout answer tied to pick frequency, not more staff, and the travel-time argument is what makes it persuasive.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: Recording a bad debt only when one specific account is judged worthless, charging it to expense in that later period — required on U.S. tax returns but unacceptable under GAAP for material amounts, because it breaks the match between the expense and the revenue that created the receivable, which the allowance method preserves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why a small firm's books disagree with its tax return, and the timing split between these two methods is the reason.

terms.definition: Holds that a firm should satisfy its target market's wants profitably only in ways that also preserve long-run consumer and social welfare — the third test the plain marketing concept leaves out — so an offering that customers genuinely want and the company profits from can still fail this standard because of the harm it does over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions that pit a profitable, popular product against a long-term harm are answered by naming this third test rather than by choosing between customers and profit.

terms.definition: The sum of a project's future cash flows discounted back to today's dollars, minus its initial cost — positive means the project earns more than the required return.
terms.whyItMatters: Capital-investment items ask whether to buy the equipment, and the sign of this figure is the answer regardless of how large the raw cash flows look.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: An INTERNAL request from a department asking purchasing to buy something, carrying no commitment to any outside party; the purchase order that purchasing then issues is the EXTERNAL document, and it is the offer that forms a binding contract when the supplier accepts it.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchasing-control questions ask which document a department head signs and which one legally obligates the company; treating the internal request as the order is the standard error.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: Cost minus salvage value, divided by total estimated lifetime output, multiplied by the units actually produced this period — expense tracks usage rather than the passage of time, so a machine that sat idle all year records none at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a press rated for 500,000 impressions and 40,000 run this year, the exam expects the per-unit rate, not the straight-line annual amount.

terms.definition: Building and maintaining relationships with professionals to exchange knowledge and opportunity.
terms.whyItMatters: Networking is essential for discovering and advancing career opportunities.

terms.definition: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price, which buys more shares when prices are low and lowers the average cost per share over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment roleplays ask how a client should handle a volatile market, and this is the answer that beats trying to time an entry point.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: A supplier-provided document in a fixed sixteen-section order under the Globally Harmonized System, covering hazards, handling, exposure controls, first aid and disposal — the fixed section order is the point, because a responder finds first-aid information in the same place on every sheet.
terms.whyItMatters: A chemical-spill roleplay expects you to say where the handling and first-aid instructions live and that the sheets must be accessible to employees on the shift, not filed in a manager's office.

terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: Cash the company has already recorded and sent to the bank that the bank has not yet posted, so it is ADDED to the bank side of a reconciliation — the opposite column from an outstanding check, which is also unposted by the bank but subtracted there, and neither one requires a journal entry on the books.
terms.whyItMatters: Reconciliation items are scored on which column they adjust and whether an entry is needed, and this pair is the one candidates reverse most often.

terms.definition: The slow divergence between a firm's strategy and its changing environment as incremental adjustments preserve old assumptions, ending in a flux period and either transformational change or failure; the danger is that performance looks fine while the gap widens.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a long-successful retailer losing ground to online rivals are scored on diagnosing the widening environment gap rather than blaming a single bad quarter.

terms.definition: The percentage used to convert a future dollar into today's dollars; raising it lowers the present value of every future cash flow and can flip a project from worth doing to not.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the input that makes a net-present-value question answerable, and exam items test that a riskier project carries a higher one.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: An arrangement where the supplier monitors the buyer's usage data and decides replenishment timing and quantity, while the buyer still owns and pays for the stock on hand — consignment differs precisely there: the supplier retains ownership until the item is sold or consumed.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays ask who should hold the replenishment decision and who carries the cash tied up in the stock; the ownership line is what separates the two arrangements.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: The depreciation schedule the Internal Revenue Code requires on tax returns, assigning each asset class a fixed recovery period and IRS table percentage under a half-year or mid-quarter convention — deliberately faster than the straight-line figure the same asset carries on the GAAP books, which is exactly what creates a deferred tax liability.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions asking why book income and taxable income differ for the same delivery truck are answered by naming this schedule and its accelerated front-loading.

terms.definition: A wrongful act or infringement of a right that causes injury and creates civil liability.
terms.whyItMatters: Businesses must understand what conduct exposes them to lawsuits and damages.

terms.definition: The yearly percentage of assets a fund charges to operate, deducted from returns automatically so the investor never sees a bill for it.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two funds with identical holdings in an investment scenario comes down to this figure, since it compounds against the client every year.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: Recordable injuries and illnesses multiplied by 200,000, divided by total hours worked — the 200,000 representing 100 full-time employees working a 2,000-hour year, which is what makes a small firm's figure comparable with a large one's.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety roleplays give an injury count and an hours-worked total and ask whether the site is above its industry benchmark; a raw injury count cannot be benchmarked and is scored as an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: A permanent write-down under ASC 360: when events suggest a long-lived asset will not recover its carrying amount, that amount is first compared with the undiscounted future cash flows the asset will generate, and only if it fails that recoverability test is it written down to fair value — a one-time loss, not the periodic allocation depreciation performs.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay scenarios about a shuttered plant still carried at cost test whether you know the write-down is required rather than optional.

terms.definition: In Aristotle's Rhetoric, the persuasive material the speaker actually invents - ethos, the character the speaker projects; pathos, the emotion produced in the audience; and logos, the reasoning inside the message. It stands against inartistic proof, which the speaker only finds and presents: contracts, testimony, laws, prior statistics. The distinction matters because a weak case is repaired by inventing better proof of the first kind, never by restating the same evidence more loudly.
terms.whyItMatters: Presentation rubrics award points across all three, so a roleplay answer that is pure data with no credibility and no audience appeal caps out even when every number is right.

terms.definition: The nominal return minus the inflation rate — what an investment actually gained in purchasing power, which can be negative while the account balance rises.
