terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a 2% savings account with 3% inflation and ask whether the saver gained; the account grew and the money bought less.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: A formal document requesting goods or services from a vendor at set terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchase orders create the paper trail for efficient procurement.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: A company's own shares bought back and held rather than retired, carried at repurchase cost as a NEGATIVE item within stockholders' equity and never as an asset. It draws no dividend and casts no vote, which is precisely why issued shares and outstanding shares stop being the same number once a buyback occurs.
terms.whyItMatters: Earnings-per-share questions require the outstanding share count, and a buyback is the event that pulls the two counts apart.

terms.definition: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict and demand judgment.
terms.whyItMatters: Recognizing and resolving dilemmas is central to leadership and compliance.

terms.definition: The total annualized return on a bond held to the end of its term, counting coupon payments plus any gain or loss between purchase price and face value.
terms.whyItMatters: A bond bought below face value returns more than its stated coupon rate, and this is the figure that shows it in an investment comparison.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: How many times inventory is sold and replaced over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Turnover reveals inventory efficiency and its impact on cash flow.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: The excess of a purchase price over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired in a business combination — recognizable only through an acquisition, never for internally built reputation — and under ASC 350 never amortized, only tested for impairment at least annually.
terms.whyItMatters: Balance-sheet questions following an acquisition ask what the large intangible line actually represents and why it does not depreciate like equipment.

terms.definition: The function that handles the individual relationship between a business and its non-union workforce — investigations, conduct issues, policy interpretation and conflict between coworkers. Labor relations, by contrast, deals with the collective relationship governed by a negotiated contract with a certified union, so a non-union employer has the first function and none of the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about building positive employer-employee relationships in a non-union business belong to this function, and misnaming it as labor relations costs the point.

terms.definition: What a sum invested today grows to by a stated date at a stated rate, computed forward with compounding rather than by adding equal yearly amounts.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-goal items give a monthly deposit and a rate and ask what the account holds in ten years; straight multiplication understates it.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: Inspecting products and services to ensure they meet set standards.
terms.whyItMatters: It catches defects early, protecting satisfaction and reducing waste.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: An outlay charged to expense in the period incurred because it only maintains an asset's existing capacity — routine repairs, servicing, replacement parts — as opposed to a capital expenditure, which extends useful life or output and is therefore added to the asset account and depreciated across the years it benefits.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you an oil-change bill and an engine-rebuild bill on the same truck and ask which one hits this year's income statement in full.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: The exposure of a bondholder to rate changes: when market rates rise, existing bonds paying the older lower rate fall in price, and longer maturities fall further.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why an investment roleplay calls long-term bonds risky for a client who may need the money early, despite the bonds being fully repaid at maturity.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The square root of (2 x annual demand x cost per order) divided by annual holding cost per unit — the single order size where rising carrying cost and falling ordering cost cross and total cost bottoms out.
terms.whyItMatters: An operations roleplay that asks you to cut the cost of holding stock is answered with this trade-off, not with 'order less': you must say that ordering more often lowers carrying cost but raises order cost, and name the quantity where the two balance.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: The private, non-governmental body that writes U.S. GAAP and publishes it as the Accounting Standards Codification, operating under SEC oversight rather than by direct statute — distinct from the International Accounting Standards Board, which issues IFRS for most of the rest of the world.
terms.whyItMatters: Regulation questions ask who actually sets the rules a U.S. company must follow, and the answer is a standard-setting board, not a government agency.

terms.definition: Invitations sent per existing user multiplied by the share of those invitations that convert into new users — 5 invites at a 25% conversion rate gives k = 1.25 — where any value above 1.0 compounds into self-sustaining growth and any value below 1.0 produces a decaying series that halts on its own once paid acquisition stops, so the threshold is exactly 1.0 and not merely 'high'.
terms.whyItMatters: A referral-program roleplay is scored on stating the break-even threshold and the two inputs you would change to reach it, not on calling the campaign shareable.

terms.definition: A contract paying a fixed stream of income for a set term or for life, bought with a lump sum — insurance against outliving savings rather than an investment for growth.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement roleplays raise it for a client who fears running out of money, and its trade-off is giving up access to the principal.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: Planning, executing, and monitoring work to hit objectives within time and budget.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets managers coordinate resources and deliver on schedule.

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: A postponement entry for cash that has already changed hands but has not yet been earned or used up — unearned revenue and prepaid assets sit on the balance sheet until the service is delivered or the benefit consumed — the exact reverse of an accrual, where the revenue or expense is recognized first and the cash follows later.
terms.whyItMatters: Adjusting-entry questions are sorted by deciding which side of this split a transaction falls on before any journal entry gets written.

terms.definition: Licensing threshold most states impose on CPA candidates: 150 semester hours of college credit — 30 beyond the 120 a bachelor's degree typically carries — plus all four sections of the Uniform CPA Exam and a year of supervised experience. Several states now allow a bachelor's degree plus two years of experience as an alternate route to the same license.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting-designations roleplay asks what a college junior must still complete before licensure; the answer is a credit count and an exam, not a job offer.

terms.definition: A basket of securities that trades on an exchange throughout the day like a single stock, unlike a mutual fund, which prices once after the market closes.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommending one over a mutual fund in an investing roleplay rests on intraday pricing and typically lower costs, not on different holdings.

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: Average daily usage multiplied by lead time in days, plus safety stock — the on-hand level that triggers a replenishment order, so it answers WHEN to order while economic order quantity answers HOW MUCH.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you daily usage, a supplier lead time and a buffer and ask at what stock level a buyer should place the reorder; picking the order size instead of the trigger level is the standard wrong answer.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: A fund fixed at a set dollar amount where every disbursement must be backed by a receipt, so vouchers plus remaining cash always equal that fixed total and replenishment is written for exactly what was spent — unlike a fluctuating fund, topped up in round sums, where a shortage simply disappears into the next refill.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash-control roleplays ask how a small office can hand out cash all week and still detect a missing twenty dollars; the fixed balance is what makes the shortage visible.

terms.definition: Raising follower motivation through vision, individualized attention, and intellectual stimulation so people exceed the stated requirement; transactional leadership instead trades contingent reward for compliance and corrects by exception, which sustains performance but rarely changes it.
terms.whyItMatters: Leadership roleplays that ask how to re-energize a team after a merger reward the transformational levers by name, with the transactional contrast used to explain why bonuses alone stalled.

terms.definition: The percentage of a covered cost the policyholder keeps paying after the deductible is met, such as 20% of every bill until an out-of-pocket maximum is reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Health-plan comparison items test that meeting the deductible does not end the client's share of the bill.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: Measures that protect confidential business and customer information from unauthorized access.
terms.whyItMatters: Good data security prevents costly breaches and keeps trust.

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: A potential obligation that depends on some future event — a pending lawsuit, a warranty claim, a loan guarantee. Under ASC 450 it is accrued as both expense and liability only when the loss is probable AND reasonably estimable; when it is merely reasonably possible it is disclosed in the notes and stays off the balance sheet entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a suit filed in November and ask whether it changes the statements or only the footnotes, and the two-condition test decides it.

terms.definition: An exclusive right granted by government to protect a new, useful invention.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must recognize what innovations a business can legally protect from copying.

terms.definition: The amount a policyholder pays out of pocket before insurance pays anything, and the lever that moves premiums — a higher one lowers the monthly cost and raises the risk carried.
terms.whyItMatters: Insurance-selection scenarios ask which policy suits a client, and the answer depends on whether they could absorb that first payment in an emergency.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Buffer units sized as a service-level z-value times the standard deviation of demand over lead time, held only to absorb variability — unlike cycle stock, which is the working quantity consumed between deliveries and would exist even with perfectly steady demand.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier-reliability roleplay turns on this: raising the promised in-stock service level raises the buffer more than proportionally, so the judge wants the cost of that extra protection weighed against the cost of a stockout.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: The IASB-issued reporting framework used across most non-U.S. markets. It is principles-based where U.S. GAAP is rules-based, bans LIFO outright, permits upward revaluation of fixed assets to fair value, and allows reversal of a prior inventory write-down — three things GAAP forbids.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions about a firm that reports in two markets test whether you can name a specific divergence rather than just assert that the frameworks differ.

terms.definition: One of the four rules Paul Grice argued every speaker in a cooperative exchange is assumed to be following: quantity (say as much as is needed and no more), quality (say only what you believe true and can support), relation (stay relevant) and manner (be brief, orderly and unambiguous). Meaning rides on a broken rule as much as a kept one - an unusually short answer to 'how did the interview go' communicates trouble precisely because it violates quantity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items about reading between the lines of a customer's reply, or about why an over-detailed email starts to sound evasive, are testing these four rules by name.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring lenders to disclose the annual percentage rate, finance charge and total payments in a standard form before a consumer signs.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why two loan offers in a roleplay can be compared at all, and why a lender quoting only a monthly payment is out of compliance.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: The ongoing expenses of running a business — labor, materials, utilities, maintenance.
terms.whyItMatters: Controlling operating costs is a lever competitors use to lift profit.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: Tax that will come due in later years because a temporary timing difference — most often faster depreciation on the return than on the books — held taxable income below book income now. It reverses in future periods, unlike a permanent difference such as a government fine, which never reverses and creates no such account.
terms.whyItMatters: Balance-sheet questions ask why a profitable firm reports a tax obligation far larger than the check it actually wrote to the IRS this year.

terms.definition: Treats emotional intelligence as a genuine intelligence with four ranked branches — perceiving emotion, using emotion to facilitate thinking, understanding how emotions combine and change, and managing emotion — and measures it with the MSCEIT, a maximum-performance test whose items are scored against consensus or expert norms instead of asking a person to rate themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that contrast the two dominant EI frameworks turn on this: this one is an ability test with scoreable answers, while the competency model is a rated inventory of habits, and picking the wrong one loses the item.

terms.definition: A deposit locked for a fixed term at a fixed rate, paying more than a savings account in exchange for a penalty on early withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-vehicle scenarios rule it out for an emergency fund precisely because the money is not reachable without giving up interest.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: Average inventory divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by 365 — the same relationship as inventory turnover but expressed as days on hand, so it falls when turnover rises and 365 divided by turnover reproduces it.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a balance sheet and a cost of goods sold figure, exam questions ask how long a firm's stock sits before selling; answering with the turnover ratio when the item asked for days is a scored miss.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: The portion of a stock issuance received above the arbitrary par amount — shares sold at $12 with a $1 par put $1 per share into the common stock account and the other $11 per share here — so only the two accounts read together show what investors actually contributed.
terms.whyItMatters: Equity-section questions give an issue price and a par value and expect the proceeds split correctly across both lines rather than dumped into one.

terms.definition: Redesigning a job by loading it vertically — handing the employee planning, decision-making and quality-checking authority previously held by a supervisor, which deepens responsibility. Job enlargement instead loads horizontally, adding more tasks at the same level of authority, and job rotation moves the person between existing jobs without changing any of them; only enrichment changes the amount of control the worker holds.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to motivate a bored experienced employee in a roleplay, adding more of the same tasks is the trap answer; the tested one is giving away supervisory decisions.

terms.definition: Federal law governing consumer credit files: it grants access to the report, sets who may pull it, and obliges a bureau to investigate a disputed item.
terms.whyItMatters: A client in a roleplay whose report shows an account they never opened has a statutory remedy under it, not just a complaint.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: Auditing a small subset of items on a rotating schedule — high-value class A lines several times a year, class C lines once — so the business keeps operating, in contrast with a full physical count, which prices accuracy by shutting the facility for a wall-to-wall count once a year.
terms.whyItMatters: In a shrink-control roleplay the judge expects you to catch record errors continuously without closing the store, and to explain why the rotating audit finds problems months earlier than the annual shutdown.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: The oversight body created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act to register, inspect, and discipline the firms that audit public companies and to set the standards those audits follow — replacing the profession's earlier self-regulation through the AICPA, which now writes standards only for private-company engagements.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and regulation questions ask what structurally changed for auditors after the accounting scandals, and the end of self-policing is the specific answer.

terms.definition: The stage requiring every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key rather than on one piece of it — a table keyed on (order_id, product_id) that also stores the customer's name breaks it, because the name follows order_id alone. It does nothing whatever when the key is a single column, since a one-column key has no part to depend on.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table already in first normal form, an exam item asks what still has to be split out; only the partial-dependency test tells the competitor which columns move to a new table.

terms.definition: Charging interest above the legal ceiling a state sets, which makes the loan itself unlawful rather than merely expensive.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the legal line separating a high-cost lender from an illegal one in consumer-credit scenarios, and the reason rate caps exist at all.
